title: A King's Feast and a Queen's Refusal
summary: Xerxes, ruler of 127 provinces from India to Cush, displays his wealth to his officials for 180 days and then holds a seven-day feast for everyone in the citadel of Susa. On the last day, merry with wine, he orders Queen Vashti to come and display her beauty to his guests, and she refuses. On the advice of his counselor Memucan, the king deposes her by an irrevocable decree and sends letters throughout the empire proclaiming that every man should be master of his own household.
story: Esther opens far from Jerusalem, in the palace of the Persian king. The first readers would have known that many Jews still lived in the eastern provinces, decades after Cyrus allowed the exiles to return home in 539/538 BC. The story of chapter 1 seems at first to have nothing to do with them. No Jew appears in it, and God is not mentioned. But the removal of Vashti opens the place that Esther will fill in chapter 2, and that placement will prove to be the hinge on which the fate of every Jew in the empire turns. The book begins by showing, without comment, how the decisions of a vain and impulsive king prepare the way for a rescue no one yet knows is needed.
historical:
Xerxes I ruled the Persian Empire from about 486 to 465 BC. The Hebrew text calls him Ahasuerus, a form of his Persian name, Khshayarsha; Xerxes is the Greek form. His empire was the largest the world had yet seen, stretching from the Indus valley (India in verse 1) to the upper Nile (Cush, roughly ancient Nubia). The 127 provinces are smaller administrative units than the twenty or so great satrapies that Greek writers describe. Susa, in the southwest of modern Iran, was one of the royal capitals, and French excavations there uncovered the palace complex with its great columned audience hall, the apadana, built by Darius I and used by Xerxes.

The third year of Xerxes' reign (verse 3) was about 483 BC. The Greek historian Herodotus records that Xerxes gathered his leading men in the years before his invasion of Greece, which began in 480 BC, and some interpreters connect the long display of chapter 1 with the preparations for that campaign, though the text itself does not say so. Herodotus names Xerxes' queen as Amestris, not Vashti or Esther; how that relates to the book is discussed in the hard question below.
cultural:
Royal banquets were a way for ancient kings to display power, reward loyalty, and bind the nobility to the throne. The description in verses 6-7, with linen hangings in white and blue, marble pillars, couches of gold and silver, and gold goblets no two alike, matches the luxury for which the Persian court was famous. Guests reclined on couches to eat. Verse 8 is compact in Hebrew, saying roughly that the drinking was by law and no one compelled. The BSB takes this to mean that there was no limit; other translations take it to mean that each guest could drink as much or as little as he chose.

The Persian king was surrounded by carefully managed layers of access. Eunuchs, castrated male servants, attended him and the royal women. The seven princes who saw the king's face (verse 14) formed an inner council; Greek writers also describe seven noble families with special privileges of access to the Persian king. The queen appeared before the king's male guests only by his command, and his demand that Vashti display herself wearing the royal crown treated her as one more of his possessions on show. Verse 19 introduces a feature of Persian law that the book will return to: a royal decree recorded among the laws of the Persians and the Medes could not be revoked (compare Daniel 6:8). Sending edicts “to each province in its own script and to each people in their own language” (verse 22) reflects the empire's genuine multilingual administration, with Aramaic as the common language of government.
literary: The chapter is a carefully crafted story with a strong note of satire. It opens with vast numbers (127 provinces, 180 days) and piles up luxury, only to show the most powerful man in the world unable to command his own wife. The king who displays “the glorious riches of his kingdom” cannot control his temper, and his response to one woman's refusal is to issue an empire-wide decree. Memucan's speech inflates a domestic embarrassment into a threat to every household in the empire. Key motifs of the whole book are introduced here: banquets and drinking, the law (dat) that cannot be revoked, royal letters sent to every province, and the king's readiness to do whatever his advisers suggest.

outline.t: Xerxes displays his wealth for 180 days
The seven-day feast in Susa and Vashti's banquet
The king summons Vashti, and she refuses
Memucan's counsel: depose the queen by law

doctrines.note: God is not named, yet the removal of Vashti prepares the way for Esther. The book invites readers to see God's quiet governance even in the careless decisions of powerful people who do not know or care about him.

The chapter shows a human king who claims vast dominion but cannot master his own anger. The irony prepares readers for the book's quiet claim that the true ruler of events is not the one on the throne in Susa.

Pride, drunkenness, and wounded vanity drive the king's actions, and his counselors turn a personal slight into public law. The chapter shows how sin in the powerful spreads outward to affect a whole empire.

words.note: Dat, law or decree. This Persian loanword appears about twenty times in Esther, far more than anywhere else in the Old Testament. It first appears in the rule about drinking (verse 8) and then in the king's question about what should be done to Vashti “according to law” (verse 15). The book will show Persian law as both powerful and easily manipulated.

Mishteh, feast or banquet, from the verb to drink. Banquets frame the whole book and mark its turning points. In this chapter the king's feasts display his power; later, Esther's banquets will become the setting in which that power is turned to save her people.

Maen, to refuse. Vashti's refusal (verse 12) is the event that sets the story in motion. The text does not explain her reasons, and interpreters have seen her either as defiant or as rightly refusing to be degraded. Either way, her refusal costs her the crown.

christ: Esther 1 contains no prophecy of the Messiah, and the link to Christ is by way of contrast and pattern. The chapter presents a king whose kingdom is displayed in wealth and whose rule is marked by pride and impulsive anger. The Gospels present a king who lays aside his glory, comes not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45), and whose kingdom is not built on display. The chapter also begins a story in which God preserves his people through events that seem to have nothing to do with him. The New Testament sees the preservation of Israel as necessary to God's promise that the Messiah would come from Abraham's line (Galatians 3:16), so even this palace drama belongs to the larger story that leads to Jesus.

hard.q: Is Esther history? Greek sources name Xerxes' queen as Amestris, not Vashti or Esther.
hard.a:
The book fits the Persian court well: the name and extent of Xerxes' empire, the palace at Susa, the royal postal system, the use of many languages, and a great deal of Persian vocabulary. But Herodotus names Xerxes' queen as Amestris, and there is no record outside the Bible of a queen named Vashti or Esther or of a vizier named Haman. Interpreters respond in several ways. Some identify Vashti with Amestris, noting that the names could be related and that Herodotus may not record every change at court; on this view Esther was a later wife who held the title of queen. Others note that Persian kings had several wives and that the Greek sources are incomplete and often hostile. Still others read Esther as a historical novella: a story set in a real court, built around real institutions and possibly a real deliverance, but shaped with the freedom of a storyteller to explain the festival of Purim.

Readers who hold different views on this question can still agree on what the book teaches: that God preserves his people even when he seems absent, and that faithfulness sometimes requires risking everything.

questions: The king displayed his wealth for six months. What do people today use to display power or importance, and what does this chapter suggest about how empty that display can be?
Vashti refused to be put on show and lost her position. When might faithfulness or dignity require saying no, even at a cost?
God is not named in this chapter, yet his purposes are moving forward. Where might God be at work in your life in ways you have not yet noticed?
